assessment:
In this preregistered study, Judd and Kievit leverage a natural experiment—the 1972 UK policy change (ROSLA) that mandated an additional year of schooling—to investigate whether education causally affects long-term brain structure. Using regression discontinuity (RD) analysis in over 30,000 UK Biobank participants, they compare individuals born just before versus just after the September 1, 1957 cutoff date, who were scanned approximately 46 years later. This design addresses a critical gap in the literature: while education is strongly associated with beneficial cognitive and neural outcomes in observational studies, causal evidence has been lacking due to pervasive confounding by socioeconomic, genetic, and selection factors. The study represents one of the first applications of rigorous causal inference methods from econometrics to population neuroimaging data.

The authors find consistently null results across all analyses. Using fuzzy local-linear RD with MSE-optimized bandwidths, they observe no discontinuity at the ROSLA cutoff for any of six global neuroimaging measures (total surface area, average cortical thickness, normalized brain volume, mean fractional anisotropy, white matter hyperintensities, or cerebrospinal fluid volume). Regional analyses of 66 cortical regions, 27 white matter tracts, and 18 subcortical structures similarly yield no significant effects after FDR correction. Bayesian local randomization analyses provide strong quantitative evidence favoring the null hypothesis (Bayes factors 11-18), robust across different prior specifications and window sizes. Importantly, the authors demonstrate that their null causal findings are not due to lack of statistical sensitivity: correlational analyses in the same participants detect associations between educational attainment and surface area, illustrating the critical distinction between causal and observational inference. Validation tests confirm ROSLA as a valid natural experiment with no evidence of manipulation around the cutoff.

The methodological rigor of this work is exceptional. The preregistered design, use of state-of-the-art RD methods with appropriate bandwidth selection, comprehensive validation tests including placebo outcomes, multiple analytical frameworks (continuity-based and local randomization), and Bayesian quantification of evidence for the null hypothesis all represent best practices in causal inference. The large sample size and comprehensive assessment across multiple brain regions and imaging modalities strengthen confidence in the findings. However, important limitations warrant consideration. The UK Biobank's healthy volunteer bias means only ~10% of the sample was actually affected by ROSLA (versus 25% in the general population), limiting statistical power and external validity to this higher-SES subpopulation. The 46-year interval between the intervention and neuroimaging, while ideal for testing theories of cumulative educational effects and 'brain reserve,' means the study cannot address whether short-term neural changes occurred and subsequently renormalized, as suggested by expansion-renormalization theories.

The findings have significant implications for theories of cognitive reserve and experience-dependent plasticity. The null results challenge prominent accounts suggesting education provides lasting neuroprotective effects detectable via conventional MRI, despite established causal effects of education on intelligence that persist across decades. The authors thoughtfully discuss potential explanations: effects may exist at microstructural resolutions below conventional MRI detection limits, initial macro-scale changes may have renormalized over time, or the neural substrates of education's cognitive benefits may not manifest as detectable structural differences. The contrast between robust causal effects on cognition and absent effects on brain structure raises important questions about the neural mechanisms underlying educational benefits. While the study cannot definitively rule out all forms of brain-education relationships, it provides compelling evidence against sustained macro-scale structural changes detectable with standard neuroimaging approaches. This work makes an important methodological contribution by demonstrating the feasibility and value of applying causal inference techniques to population neuroscience, potentially moving the field beyond purely correlational approaches.
